nameStory: The "alternate-leaved" part of this dogwood's name tells you exactly what makes it special among its relatives - it's the only dogwood in our region with leaves arranged alternately along the stem rather than in pairs. It's also called pagoda dogwood because its horizontal branches create distinctive tiers that look like the levels of a Japanese pagoda. The "dogwood" family name comes from "dag wood" - dag being an old English word for skewer, referring to the hard wood that was perfect for making arrows and tool handles.
description: Alternate-leaved dogwood is a small understory tree or large shrub that typically grows 15-25 feet tall in New England forests. It has a distinctive layered, horizontal branching pattern that creates an elegant tiered appearance. The smooth-edged leaves are arranged alternately along reddish stems, and in late spring it produces clusters of small, creamy-white flowers followed by blue-black berries on bright red stalks. This native species prefers the dappled shade of mature forests and is an important food source for birds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged alternately along the stem (not in pairs like other dogwoods), with smooth edges and prominent curved veins that follow the leaf's oval shape. Touch them - they feel smooth and slightly waxy on top.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctive horizontal, layered branching creates a pagoda-like silhouette with tiers of foliage. Young stems are often reddish and feel smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters at branch tips in late May to early June. Each tiny flower has four petals and gives off a faintly sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue to blue-black berries appear in late summer on distinctive bright red or pink stalks that feel slightly sticky. The colorful stalks make the dark berries really pop visually.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, dark gray bark on mature trunks with shallow furrows. Young branches have a reddish tinge that's especially noticeable in winter light.

habitat: Look for alternate-leaved dogwood in the understory of mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially on slopes and in ravines with rich, moist, well-drained soil. It thrives in partial shade beneath maples, oaks, and other canopy trees, often growing alongside witch hazel, elderberry, and ferns. You'll find it from sea level up to about 3,000 feet in elevation.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in May with a fresh green color, followed by clusters of small white flowers in late May to early June that attract small pollinators like flies and beetles.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage shows off the distinctive tiered branching pattern, and blue berries begin forming on reddish stalks by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to reddish-purple, and the dark blue berries on bright red stalks create a striking color combination that birds love.
seasonality.winter: The horizontal branching pattern and reddish young twigs are most visible, along with the smooth gray bark and small clustered buds.

funFact: This tree is like nature's bird buffet table - its berries are eaten by over 40 species of birds, and its layered branch structure provides perfect nesting platforms at different heights, making it a one-stop shop for our feathered friends!
confusionNotes: The alternate leaf arrangement instantly separates this from all other New England dogwoods, which have leaves in pairs (opposite). If you're ever unsure, just check the leaves - if they're alternate, you've found the pagoda dogwood! Remember: "Alternate arrangement = pagoda dogwood."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "dogwood," this species is quite different from the showy flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) that many people know from landscaping - that one has large white "petals" (actually bracts) while alternate-leaved dogwood has tiny clustered flowers. Both are native, but alternate-leaved dogwood is much more common in New England's wild forests.
compareHints: Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves. The tiered, horizontal branching also sets it apart from other dogwoods like red osier (which grows in wet areas with red stems) or gray dogwood (which has a more upright, less layered growth habit). The blue berries on red stalks are also distinctive compared to the white berries of gray dogwood or red berries of flowering dogwood.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
